paras: The flogging of John Brown was an attack by a posse of local citizens on a Black man near Fort Madison, South Carolina, on the night of Thursday, July 2, 1903. Accused of attempting to assault a white woman, Brown was tied to a trestle, whipped, and released on a promise to leave South Carolina for good. The only account, a Seneca dispatch, presented the flogging as an alternative to lynching.

According to the dispatch, 'news' reached Seneca that Brown, called 'a negro,' had attempted to assault 'a prominent white woman' at Fort Madison, about twenty miles away. He was captured by 'a posse of the leading citizens of that community' and taken to a trestle about a mile from Madison, where he was tied to the woodwork with ropes and chains. The men then whipped him on his bare body with hickory sprouts, which were later said to carry 'hair, flesh and blood.'

The dispatch claimed that Brown would have been lynched had some of the crowd not urged the others to whip and free him instead. Beaten so badly he could hardly walk, he was released after promising never again to set foot in South Carolina. The report added that he was 'a desperate character' who had served chain-gang sentences in South Carolina and other states.

The Raleigh printing closed by saying excitement had run high for several hours but that all was now quiet. No report of arrests, an investigation, or of Brown's later whereabouts appears in the coverage.

The story circulated as a single dispatch under the headline 'Flogged Him and Let Him Go.' The Raleigh News & Observer ran it on July 7 with credit to the Charleston News and Courier, and the Keowee Courier of Pickens Court House printed it without credit twice in its July 8 issue, on pages 3 and 4. Both versions stated the accusation as fact and twice called Brown 'the brute,' while describing the whipping in graphic detail.
Coverage was confined to these white papers; no Black-press account of the flogging was found.

reader.title: Flogging of John Brown
bases: A 'posse of the leading citizens' seized a man accused of a crime, flogged him at a trestle and freed him on a promise to leave the state; no organized band or night-riding is described, so this is a mob flogging rather than whitecapping (A1, A2).
All three printings carry one Seneca dispatch of July 5 credited to the Charleston News and Courier; no independent report was found (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Seneca dispatch (Charleston News and Courier)
accounts.gist: Relays 'news' reaching Seneca that Brown attempted an assault, was captured by leading citizens, flogged at a trestle and freed on a promise to leave the state, and that he would have been lynched but for members of the crowd who urged the lash instead.

framing.detail: Under the headline 'Flogged Him and Let Him Go,' the dispatch states the assault attempt as fact, calls Brown 'the brute' and 'a desperate character,' and casts the flogging as a lesser course than lynching.
The Raleigh News & Observer ran the dispatch with credit to the Charleston News and Courier; the Keowee Courier printed it twice in one issue without credit.

seizure, binding to a trestle, whipping, and forced departure from the state; no pursuit is described

white: 3 printings in 2 papers (Raleigh, July 7; Keowee Courier, July 8, twice), all one dispatch

info: Thursday night before a July 5 dispatch, i.e. July 2, 1903

sources.note: 'Flogged Him and Let Him Go,' credited to the Charleston News and Courier, Seneca, S.C., July 5 dispatch; fullest text, ends 'Everything is said to be quiet there now.'
quotes: The negro was captured by a posse of the leading citizens of that community and taken to a trestle, about a mile from Madison, tied with ropes and chains to the woodwork
Doubtless he would have been lynched if some of the crowd had not urged them to give him the lash and free him, and not lynch him.
He was freed by the mob, by making a promise that he would never put his foot on the soil of South Carolina again.
It is said that where hickory sprouts were found hair, flesh and blood was found on them.
